verses.translation_literal: Judge me, O God, and plead my plea from [a] nation not faithful; from [a] man of deceit and of injustice you will rescue me.
verses.translation_dramatic: Judge me, O God. Take up my case, for I have no strength to argue it myself. Set it against a nation with no loyalty in it, no covenant-faithfulness, and lift me out of the grip of the man whose trade is lies and whose law is wrong. You, who see through both, rescue me.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a courtroom prayer, and the actor should play it as one. The verb 'judge' (shafat) in the ancient Near East meant to give a verdict and to put right, so 'judge me' asks for vindication, not for scrutiny. The second verb repeats a root: 'plead my plea' (riva riv-i). The Hebrew keeps the lawsuit word twice in a row, and the KJV's 'plead my cause' keeps it only once. The speaker has no human advocate and no power to enforce a ruling, so God must be both advocate and judge.

The KJV 'ungodly nation' is too religious and too soft. The Hebrew says 'a nation not chasid', that is, without chesed, the loyal love that holds a community together; the failing is a lack of faithfulness and mercy, not just of piety. And 'the deceitful and unjust man' turns a construction ('man of deceit and injustice') into two adjectives and loses the picture of a man defined by his fraud. The final verb, tefalleteni, is an imperfect, so YLT's 'Thou dost deliver me' is possible, but after two imperatives it reads as a plea. The psalm does not say who the nation is: Rashi says Edom, Radak the Babylonians, Malbim philosophers who mislead people about faith.

philological_notes.note: From chesed, loyal love or covenant faithfulness. 'Not chasid' means a people with no loyalty or mercy toward others, a stronger charge than 'ungodly'.
A verb and its own noun side by side: 'argue my argument'. It is the language of a legal dispute, with God as the one who takes up the case.
'Let me escape, get me away safe'. Metzudat Zion links it to 'songs of deliverance' (rannei palet, Psalm 32:7).

verses.translation_literal: For you [are] God of my refuge; why have you cast me off? Why, darkened, do I walk about in [the] oppression of [an] enemy?
verses.translation_dramatic: For you are the God who is my stronghold. Then why have you thrown me away? Why must I walk about in black, head bowed, with the enemy's hand pressing on my back?
verses.directors_commentary:
Verse 1 asked for a verdict; verse 2 is the complaint behind it, and it has a hinge. 'For you are the God of my refuge' is a statement of trust, and the very next word is a question that seems to deny it. Play the whiplash, not a calm theological puzzle. Ma'oz is a fortress, a place where you can hold out, not just 'strength' as in the KJV, which loses the picture of walls. Zanach, 'cast off', is the word for throwing something away as useless.

The Hebrew qoder means 'darkened, black', and the English 'mourning' is a fair reading: a person in mourning dressed in dark clothes and went about unwashed. The KJV's 'because of the oppression' makes the grief caused by the enemy; the Hebrew simply says he walks 'in' it, as if it were the air around him. Lachats, 'oppression', is a squeeze or pressure. Two 'why's open the two halves, in the same position, so the repetition is a drumbeat. Ibn Ezra reads the 'for' as: I have no strength to take my judgment from him except in you.

philological_notes.note: A fortress, a place of safety in war; the root means strength. 'Stronghold' is closer to the picture than the KJV's abstract 'strength'.
From a root meaning to be dark or dusky; Metzudat Zion glosses it 'dark and black'. It is the grief of a person who has put on dark clothes, and it sets up the 'light' of verse 3.

verses.translation_literal: Send your light and your truth; they, they-may-lead-me; they-may-bring-me to [the] mountain of your holiness and to your dwelling-places.
verses.translation_dramatic: Send out your light. Send out your truth. Let them be the ones who take me by the hand and lead me, the ones who carry me home, up to your holy mountain, to the place where you dwell.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker has just said that he walks in black, with the enemy pressing on him (verse 2). Now the colour flips: the cure for that darkness is not rescue by force but light, and light that arrives as a companion. The two gifts are named as if they were messengers or guides: 'light' ('or) and 'truth' ('emet, with the sense of reliability, faithfulness). Hebrew then makes them do something no English article can: hemmah, 'they', is one independent pronoun set before a verb that already says 'they' in its ending (yanchuni, 'they lead me'). Hebrew does not need the extra pronoun, so its presence points a finger: these two, and no one else. YLT catches the effect with 'They--they lead me'. Play it as a gesture toward the two things he has just called down, almost as if he can already see them walking toward him.

The KJV smooths this in several ways. It writes 'let them lead me; let them bring me', which makes a courteous permission out of two verbs that are pleas in the plain voice of need, and it drops the pointing pronoun altogether. 'Thy holy hill' flattens har qodshekha, literally 'the mountain of your holiness': Zion is not simply a sacred hill but the mountain made up of God's own holiness. And 'tabernacles' is an old-fashioned word for mishkenot, the plural of mishkan, 'dwelling places', the same word used for the desert sanctuary; the plural suggests the whole precinct, not a single tent. In verse 4 these names become an altar and a place to play the lyre, so the journey is physical and ends in worship. For a modern speaker, this is homesickness: an exile or a man shut out of the temple wants to be led back by a guide he trusts.

philological_notes.note: The independent third-person plural pronoun. Hebrew verbs already carry their subject, so a separate pronoun before the verb (hemmah yanchuni) puts weight on the subject: 'they, and they alone, will lead me'. Radak glosses the clause simply as 'let them bring me' (yevi'uni), reading the pair of verbs as parallel.

'They lead me', the verb for guiding a person along a route, not for driving a flock. Metzudat Zion ties it to the same root in Exodus 13:17, where God 'did not lead' Israel by the Philistine road. The exodus echo fits a prayer to be guided home.

Plural of mishkan, 'dwelling place', from the root meaning to settle or tent. The plural is common in the Psalms for the sanctuary precinct with its several buildings and courts; Ibn Ezra reads it as the courts of a future temple. KJV 'tabernacles' is accurate but now sounds like a feast.

verses.translation_literal: And I will come to [the] altar of God, to God, [the] joy of my rejoicing; and I will give thanks to you with [a] lyre, God, my God.
verses.translation_dramatic: And then I will come in to the altar of God, to God himself, the gladness at the heart of my gladness. And there, with the strings under my fingers, I will give you thanks, O God, my God.
verses.directors_commentary:
The journey of verse 3 arrives at the altar, and here the verse changes from request to promise. The verb ve'avo'ah is a cohortative: 'let me come, I will come', with a strong will in it. The altar is where thanksgiving and sacrifice are offered; Malbim reads that once the speaker is brought there, he himself will bring offerings. Then the 'God' title is doubled, 'to God, the joy of my rejoicing'.

The KJV's 'my exceeding joy' smooths a Hebrew phrase that piles up two joy-words, simchat gili, 'the joy of my jubilation'. Gil is shouting joy, so the picture is of someone leaping, not of mild satisfaction. 'Harp' in the KJV renders kinnor, which was a small hand-held lyre, played by plucking; the Levites used it in the sanctuary. The closing 'O God, my God' (Elohim Elohai) echoes the opening 'O God' of verse 1 and ends the verse with a personal claim: not just 'God' but 'my God'. Rashi reads 'I will thank you with the lyre' as thanks for having been brought out.

philological_notes.note: Two joy-words in a construct chain: 'the joy of my exulting'. Gil is loud, bodily rejoicing; the phrase makes God himself the source of that joy.
A hand-held stringed instrument, a lyre, not the large concert harp of the English 'harp'.

verses.translation_literal: Why are you bowed down, my soul, and why do you murmur upon me? Wait for God, for yet I will give thanks to him, [the] salvations of my face and my God.
verses.translation_dramatic: Why, my soul, are you bent so low? Why do you moan and churn within me? Wait. Wait for God, for I will yet give him thanks, the one who saves my face, who is my God.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker turns from God to himself and speaks to his own soul, nefesh, here the whole self that feels. Make it tender, a little firm, like talking down someone in panic. Two 'why's again, but now they are aimed inward, and the answer is a single imperative: 'wait' (hochili). Hebrew 'wait' (yachal) is not passive; it is hope, a taut waiting for something that will come.

The KJV 'cast down' and 'disquieted' are archaic. Tishtochachi means to be bowed or bent low, and tehemi means to murmur or growl, a word used of the sea and of the sound of a crowd, so the soul is restless and noisy. The last phrase is the puzzle. Yeshuot panai is 'the salvations of my face': the face is what shows grief or joy, so God is the one who turns a fallen face upward. The KJV 'health of my countenance' is a leftover of the older sense of 'health'; ASV's 'help' is closer, but both lose the plural. This verse is the refrain that also closes Psalm 42 (verses 6 and 12), and Psalms 42 and 43 are often read together as one poem (Meiri says as much); the repeated words are the speaker's own refrain.

philological_notes.note: To bow down, to sink low; here a reflexive form, 'you bend yourself down'. YLT's 'bowest thou thyself' shows it.
To growl, murmur, be in uproar; used of a crowd and of the sea. The soul is turbulent, and this is the sound it makes.
To wait with expectation, to hope. It is an imperative addressed to the soul, as if to a tired child.
A plural noun: 'salvations of my face'. The face shows the state of the person; God is the one who brings deliverance that shows on it.
